title: Managing a Python Installation
section: The Golden Rule of Python Environments
text:
The Golden Rule of Python Environments
When you want to install a package for Python (like pandas), many guides often tell you to open the terminal and type pip install pandas. Do not do this.
Operating systems like MacOS and Linux rely on a hidden, system-level Python installation to run core operating system background tasks. If you use global pip to install or upgrade packages, you risk overwriting the dependencies your operating system relies on. This leads to a broken OS, or at best, conflicting dependencies between your own projects (often called “Dependency Hell”).
Preventing Dependecy Hell: Every project must live in its own isolated “Virtual Environment.”
This is one of the downsides to Python, in order to prevent dependency conflicts you need to manage what amounts to different Python installations. Fortunately, there are solutions that make this less tedious and prone to complication.

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
uv
Historically, managing Python safely required juggling several different tools (pyenv for Python versions, venv for environments, pip for packages, and pipx for global apps).
There are multiple solutions to managing different Python installations (Conda/Miniconda are very popular), a recent one is uv. This replaces all of the traditional tools with a single tool. It operates entirely in user-space, meaning it requires no administrator privileges and generally can be installed without friction on computers that you do not have full control over.

1. Installing uv
Open your terminal and run the official standalone installer:
# On macOS/Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# On Windows
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | more"


2. Installing Python Versions
You do not need to download Python from the official website. uv will download and isolate whatever version of Python you need for a project.
For example, if you need a Python version of 3.12 as a requirement:
# Install the latest version of Python 3.12
uv python install 3.12


3. Creating a Project
When creating a new project, uv makes environment isolation automatic.
# Create a new project directory
mkdir data_analysis_project
cd data_analysis_project

# Initialize the project structure
uv init

# Add a package (this automatically creates the virtual environment!)
uv add pandas matplotlib
Notice that we never had to manually “activate” an environment. By using uv add, the tool automatically handles the creation and linkage of the isolated environment.


4. Running Your Code
To run a script using the isolated environment, simply prefix your command with uv run.
# Runs script.py using the isolated pandas/matplotlib installation
uv run script.py

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Installing Global Tools
Sometimes you need to install a Python application that you want to use everywhere, not just in one project. A good example is something like Jupyter Lab.
Installing an application into a specific project’s virtual environment is tedious, but installing them globally via pip breaks the Golden Rule.
The solution is an isolated tool runner.
# Install Jupyter Lab in its own isolated global environment
uv tool install jupyterlab

# You can now launch Jupyter from anywhere on your computer
jupyter lab
If you are working on a legacy system without uv, the traditional equivalent of this command is pipx install jupyterlab.

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Working with Older Codebases
While uv is the modern standard, you will inevitably encounter older codebases or tutorials that use the standard library tools. Adjusting them to use uv is straightforward.
If a repository contains a requirements.txt file, the traditional setup workflow looks like this:

Create the Environment:

python3 -m venv .venv

Activate the Environment: (You must do this every time you open a new terminal)

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate

Install the Dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Deactivate:

deactivate

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Recap
Need a library for a script? (e.g., numpy, pandas) -> Use uv add or a local venv.
Need a standalone app? (e.g., jupyter) -> Use uv tool install or pipx.
Never use: pip install [package] outside of an active virtual environment.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Types of Files
Data is stored in many formats, but in most cases we are concerned with two major types of files:

Text file: contains data that has been encoded as text (human readable).
Binary file: contains data that has been encoded in binary (not human readable).

To simplify testing our code, we will focus almost entirely on text files for our discussion on File Input and Output.
The filename extension is a short sequence of characters that appear at the end of a filename preceded by a period. The extension indicates the type of data stored in the file.

The .txt extension indicates a text file.
There are many extension names for binary files, but a common one is .bin.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
File Access Methods
There are two primary ways to access data stored in file:

Sequential access: the file read sequentially from beginning to end and we cannot skip ahead
Direct access: we can jump directly to any piece of data in the file

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
File Objects
In Python the file object is the object associated with a specific file. Multiple files can be active at the same type and the file objects will each hold their respective file’s data. This object is referenced by a variable and we can use specific methods related to files to help read and write data to it.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Opening a File
Our first step is always opening a file. The open function creates a file object and associates it with that specific file.
General format: file_object= open(filename, mode)
The mode is a string that specifies for what purpose the file will be opened. There are three major operations when it comes to files:

Reading (‘r’)
Writing (‘w’)
Appending (‘a’)


Specifying the Location of a File
If the open function receives a filename that does not contain a filepath, Python will assume that the file is in the same directory as the program. Mistyping the location is a common source of errors.
If the program is running and a file is created, it is created by default in the same directory as the program. We can specify an alternative path and file name in the open function argument.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Writing Data to a File
We use a file object’s write method used to write data to the file.
Format: file_variable.write(string)
When we are done writing, we need to close the file object using its close method.
Format: file_variable.close()

Concatenating a Newline to and Stripping it From a String
In most cases, data items written to a file are values referenced by variables. But all data that will be written to a standard text file needs to be in string format. But even with data that is in string format it is often needed to concatenate a \n to data before writing it. Remember that this is the newline character and so is used to place each piece of data on its own separate line.
Similarly, we often need to remove the newline from a string after it is read from the file. We can do this easily using the string processing methods we learned earlier. Specifically, we can use the rstrip method to strip the newline character from the end of the string.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
#This writes Line 1, Line 2, … to the file.

file = open("example.txt", "w")

for i in range(1, 6):
    file.write(f"Line {i}\n")

file.close()

Write the odd numbers from 1 to 15 (inclusive) to file named numbers.txt


Click to show answer

file = open("numbers.txt", "w")

for i in range(1, 16):
  if i % 2 == 1:
    file.write(f"{i}\n")

file.close()

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Reading Data From a File
We have to primary methods when it comes to reading data from a file.
The first is the read method, which reads the entire file contents into memory. This only works if the file has been opened for reading and all the contents are returned as a single string. In general, this is cumbersome as you will need to process the large string containing the entire contents of the file to separate out the information you are interested in.
The second method is the readline method, which reads line by line from a file object and returns the contents of each line as a string. Note that the newline character will be present. The readline method uses an empty string as a sentinel when end of file is reached. Using readline is done with a while loop with the format: while line != ''.
file = open("example.txt", "r")

while (line := file.readline()) != "":
    print(line)
file.close()

File Pointers
Python keeps track of the current location we are at in the file using a file pointer. When the file is opened, the file pointer is set to the beginning of the file. In our example above we then use the readline method, this reads characters until a newline is encountered. Calling the readline method again advances the file pointer to the next newline, and so on until we reach the end of the file (signified by the empty string).
We have the capability to move the file pointer ourselves using the seek method. For example, seek(0) moves the file pointer to the start of the file. This can be very useful when it comes to opening files for both reading and writing which we will see later on.


Using Python’s for Loop to Read Lines
In practice, we tend to use for loops to iterate through a file automatically. Python is structured that we can use simple syntax to start automatically at the beginning of the file and progress line by line to the end.
Format:
for line in file_object:
    statement
    statement
    ...
for loop syntax automatically pulls each line from our file (line is just the target variable for the for loop). Note that the rstrip here prevents us from having two newlines (there is one implicitly associated with print and rstrip removes the one that was added in the writing process).
file = open("example.txt", "r")

for line in file:
    print(line.rstrip('\n'))

file.close()

Read from the file numbers.txt and add one to each number before it is printed.


Click to show answer

file = open("numbers.txt", "r")

for line in file:
    print(int(line.rstrip('\n'))+1)

file.close()

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Appending Data to an Existing File
text:
Appending Data to an Existing File
When we open a file with w mode, if the file already exists it is overwritten. All data within the file is erased and we start from an empty file.
If we want to keep data that is already in a file, we can append it using the a mode. All data written is written to the current end of the file.
#This example writes Line 1, Line 2, … etc to an existing file and places the new content after any existing content.


file = open("example.txt", "a")

    for i in range(1, 6):
        file.write(f"Line {i}\n")

file.close()

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Combining Reading and Writing
We are not restricted to a single mode when opening a file. Python allows us the option to open files with the capacity to perform multiple tasks.
The + symbol adds reading or writing to a file mode.

‘r+’ → read and write

File must already exist
File pointer starts at the beginning
Writing happens at the current file position
Writing will still overwrite existing content

‘w+’ → write and read

Deletes all existing contents when the file is opened
If the file does not exist, it is created
File pointer starts at the beginning

‘a+’ → append and read

File is created if it does not exist
File pointer starts at the end
Writing always adds to the end
Reading requires moving the file pointer manually


file = open("data.txt", “a+")

for i in range(1, 6):
    file.write(f"Line {i}\n")

for line in file:
    print(line.rstrip('\n'))

file.close()
In the example above we initial write lines to a file data. The file pointer is now at the end of the file.
We then attempt to read from the file, but as the file pointer is at the end, the read loop starts at the end and so nothing is printed.
Note that this is not an error, it is expected behavior. We can only read what the file point passes over.
We can alter our example here to move the file pointer back to the beginning so we can read the file we have just written.
file = open("example.txt", “a+")

for i in range(1, 6):
    file.write(f"Line {i}\n")

file.seek(0)

for line in file:
    print(line.rstrip('\n'))

file.close()

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Using the with Statement to Open Files
text:
Using the with Statement to Open Files
The with statement can be used to open a file and automatically close the file.
General format:
with open(filename, mode) as file_variable:
    statement
    statement
    ...

filename is a string specifying the name of the file
mode is a string specifying the mode, such as ‘r’, ‘w’, or ‘a’
file_variable is the name of the variable that will reference the file object
The indented block of statements is known as the with suite

with open("example.txt", "w") as file:

for i in range(1, 6):
    file.write(f"Line {i}\n")

Opening Multiple Files
We can open multiple files at the same time and the with keyword becomes very useful (but not required) as we can avoid keeping track of when and if our possibly many different files are closed.
This example opens two files for the purpose of copying the data from the first file (file1) to the second file (file2).
with open('file1.txt', 'r') as input_file, open('file2.txt', 'w') as output_file:

for line in input_file:
    output_file.write(line)

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Displaying an Exception’s Default Error Message
text:
Displaying an Exception’s Default Error Message
An exception object is an object created in memory when an exception is thrown. It usually contains a default error message pertaining to the exception.
We can assign the exception object to a variable in an except clause using the following format: except ErrorType as name:
We can also pass the exception object variable to print function to display the default error message.
try:
    print(variable)

except NameError as e:
    print(e)
    print("Continuing on")

Given the list [1,2,’3’,4,’5’,6], use a for loop to attempt to add each element into an accumulator variable.
Use exception handling (use TypeError as the exception type) to ignore errors for undefined operations.


Click to show answer

var = [1,2,'3',4,'5',6]
s = 0

for i in var:
    try:
        s += i
    except TypeError as e:
        print(e)
        continue

print(s)

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Handling Multiple Exceptions
Often the code in the try suite can throw more than one type of exception. We can write multiple except clauses, one for each type of exception that needs to be handled.
In this example we can catch two specific errors, a ValueError where the input is not a number and a ZeroDivisionError where the input is a zero. Each error is handled separately.
try:

    num = int(input())
    result = 10 / num
    print(result)

except ValueError:
    print(”Invalid Number.")

except ZeroDivisionError:
    print(”Zero Division.")
Note that an except clause that does not list a specific exception will handle any exception that is raised in the try suite. This may sound advantageous as it reduces the amount of code that needs to be written but can cause problems in the future when debugging as any exception will be caught (including ones you did not anticipate). Your program will continue to run after that step but there may be substantial corruption of things that come afterwards due to unintended behavior.
It is generally considered bad form to have a catch-all exception block. Instead, you should only handle exceptions that you anticipate on occurring. This will allow you to properly debug errors that you did not anticipate.
This example handles all exceptions but the lack of exception type removes useful information as to what went wrong.
try:
    num = int(input())
    result = 10 / num
    print(result)

except:
    print("An error occurred.")

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
13: Exceptions and Files
text:
The finally Clause
A try/except statement may include an optional finally clause, which appears after all the except clauses. The statements in a finally clause will execute regardless if an exception occurs. These are often used to perform some kind of cleanup before exiting like closing a file.
General format:
try:
    statement
    statement
    ...

except:
    statement
    statement
    ...

finally:
    statement
    statement
    ...
In this example the try block attempts to open and read the file. The except block handles the case where the file does not exist. And the finally block ensures that the file is closed if it was successfully opened.
try:
    file = open("data.txt", "r")

except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Error: The file does not exist.")

finally:
    try:
        file.close()
    except NameError:
        pass

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: What If an Exception Is Not Handled?
text:
What If an Exception Is Not Handled?
We have encountered this throughout all the previous content. Unhandled exceptions cause the program to halt and provide a default error message.
When it comes to using a try/except suite, exceptions can still go unhandled if we do not have an except clause that specifies the exception of the correct type or an exception is raised outside the try/except suite altogether.

title: 11: Dictionaries
text:
Dictionaries
Dictionaries are another type of object that stores a collection of data. What makes them different from the other data structures we have seen so far is that each element is actually two parts: a key and a value.

Often referred to as mapping of key to value
Key must be an immutable object like an integer or a string

To retrieve a specific value, we use the key associated with it.
The format for creating a dictionary is: dictionary= {key1:val1, key2:val2}

# Creating a dictionary with fruit names as keys and quantities as values

fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

Adding Elements to an Existing Dictionary

Dictionaries are mutable objects
To add a new key-value pair: dictionary[key] = value
If key exists in the dictionary, the value associated with it will be changed


fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,

}

del fruit_counts['cherry']

Creating an Empty Dictionary and Using for Loop to Iterate Over a Dictionary

title: 11: Dictionaries
text:
Some Common Dictionary Methods

clear method: deletes all the elements in a dictionary, leaving it empty

Format: dictionary.clear()

get method: gets a value associated with specified key from the dictionary

Format: dictionary.get(key, default)

default is returned if key is not found

Alternative to [] operator

Cannot raise KeyError exception




fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

print(fruit_counts.get('mango',-1))

-1



items method: returns all the dictionaries keys and associated values

Format: dictionary.items()
Returned as a dictionary view

Each element in dictionary view is a tuple which contains a key and its associated value
Use a for loop to iterate over the tuples in the sequence

Can use a variable which receives a tuple, or can use two variables which receive key and value





fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

for key, value in fruit_counts.items():
  print(key, value, end='\t')

apple 4 banana 2    cherry 10   



keys method: returns all the dictionaries keys as a sequence

Format: dictionary.keys()

pop method: returns value associated with specified key and removes that key-value pair from the dictionary

Format: dictionary.pop(key, default)

default is returned if key is not found


popitem method: Returns, as a tuple, the key-value pair that was last added to the dictionary. The method also removes the key-value pair from the dictionary.

Format: dictionary.popitem()
Key-value pair returned as a tuple

values method: returns all the dictionaries values as a sequence

Format: dictionary.values()
Use a for loop to iterate over the values


Table of some common dictionary methods







Method
Description




clear
Clears the contents of a dictionary.


get
Gets the value associated with a specified key. If the key is not found, the method does not raise an exception. Instead, it returns a default value.


items
Returns all the keys in a dictionary and their associated values as a sequence of tuples.


keys
Returns all the keys in a dictionary as a sequence of tuples.


pop
Returns the value associated with a specified key and removes that key-value pair from the dictionary. If the key is not found, the method returns a default value.


popitem
Returns, as a tuple, the key-value pair that was last added to the dictionary. The method also removes the key-value pair from the dictionary.


values
Returns all the values in the dictionary as a sequence of tuples.

title: 11: Dictionaries
section: The Dictionary Merge Operator (Python 3.9 or higher)
text:
The Dictionary Merge Operator (Python 3.9 or higher)

The dictionary merge operator is the | symbol
It merges two dictionaries into a single dictionary that is the combination of the two
dict3 = dict1 | dict2

After this statement, dict3 will have all the elements of dict1 and dict2
If the same key appears in dict1 and dict2, the new dictionary keeps the value from the dictionary on the right-hand side of the | operator (in this case, dict2).



d1= {"apple": 4}
d2= {"banana": 2}

d3 = d1 | d2

print(d3)

{'apple': 4, 'banana': 2}

5: Functions
text:
We have used prebuilt functions repeatedly in this course (like print or input) and now we will look at building our own.
A function is a group of statements within a program that performs a specific task. This collection of statements is attached to a name, and the name can be used to perform those statements repeatedly without having to duplicate the underlying code.
This idea of code reuse is a primary benefit of functions. We get to write the code once then call it as many times as needed. This appreciably simplifies our codebase as it reduces duplicate code and this results in superior testing and debugged as we only need to test and debug just a single block of code, the function itself.


Function naming rules are very similar to those of variables:

Cannot use keywords as a function name
Cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or underscore
All other characters must be a letter, number or underscore
Uppercase and lowercase characters are distinct

And like variables, the function name should be descriptive of the task carried out by the function.




Defining a function:
def function_name(parameter_1,parameter_2, ...):
    statement_1
    statement_2
    ...

The function header is the first line of the function and includes the keyword def and the name of the function. This is followed by parentheses where the (optional) parameters needed by the function are placed and then ended with a colon.
Inside the function we have the statement or statements that you want the function to perform. Note that the statements inside the function must be indented.



To use a function, we call it by invoking its name.

def add(x,y):
    print(x + y)

add(2,3)

5


The simple function add above takes in two parameters, x and y then prints their summed value. A parameter is a variable that is assigned the value of an argument when the function is called. We call the function with specific values for the parameters, arguments, in this case 2 and 3 using the notation add(2,3). Note that the function assigns the parameter values in order of the arguments that are passed in. 2 is the first argument, so it is assigned to x and 3 is the second argument so it is assigned to y.
Functions can take in multiple arguments, a single argument or none at all. How many parameters are needed for a function is dependent on its construction.



The function we just saw does not return any data back out of the function, it simply prints a value to the terminal. We call this type of function that executes the statements it contains and then ends a void function.
In contrast, a value-returning function executes its statements and then returns some value back to the point of the program that called it. The input and int functions are example of value-returning functions that you have used.
To return a value from a function, you need only use the return keyword.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

5


We can see in the modified version of our add function that we now return the sum of the values instead of printing to the terminal. This returned value is stored in the result variable and then this variable is printed to the terminal. Note that we do not need to tell Python what type of value is being returned unlike in some other programming languages. The return keyword only specifics to send that value back, there is no check to see what type of value it actually is.


We can return multiple values by separating the values by commas.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

(5, 2, 3)


Our add function now returns the sum, then the value associated with parameter x and finally the value associated with parameter y. Note that the values are returned in the order they are specified. Also note that the variable result is now a tuple containing three objects, which is what we would expect since we returned three individual values.
We can assign these values immediately using the convention for multiple assignment:

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result, x, y = add(2,3)
print(result)
print(x)
print(y)

5
2
3


If you choose to do multiple assignment from a function call, you will need exactly as many variables as there are returned values.



You can use the pass keyword to create empty functions. This keyword is ignored by the Python interpreter and this can be helpful when designing a program.

def a_function():
    pass





Changes made to a parameter value within the function do not affect the argument. This is known as pass by value and it provides a way for unidirectional communication between one function and another function.

def function_1():
    value = 5
    print(f'The value is {value}')
    function_2(value)
    print(f'The value is {value}')

def function_2(x):
    print(f'The value is {x}')
    x = 0
    print(f'The value is now {x}')

Note that in this example the value in the first function is passed to the second function, but the change is not reflected in the first function. The second function gets a copy of data in the first value and not the actual variable itself.


A keyword argument is an argument that specifies which parameter the value should be passed to.
function_name(parameter=value)
Note that the position when calling the function is not relevant. It is also possible to mix keyword arguments and positional arguments when calling a function but all positional arguments must appear first.
Keyword arguments are often used to provide a default argument for a parameter. A default argument is a value that will be there by default unless explicitly overwritten when the function is called.
In the following example we can omit passing a value into the tax rate parameter because a default argument is provided. We are still free to overwrite it whenever we need.

def show_tax(price, tax_rate=0.08):
    tax = price * tax_rate
    print(f'The tax is {tax}.')

show_tax(10)

show_tax(10,tax_rate=0.10)

The tax is 0.8.
The tax is 1.0.






In Python, scope determines the visibility and lifetime of a variable. That is, scope is the part of a program in which a variable may be accessed.
Python follows the LEGB rule, which defines the order in which the interpreter searches for a variable name.

Local
Enclosing
Global
Built-in



A local variable is variable that is assigned a value inside a function. It belongs to the function in which it was created.
Only statements inside that function can access it, an error will occur if another function tries to access the variable. The scope of a local variable is the function where it was created and any local variables are destroyed when their associated function ends.
A local variable cannot be accessed by statements inside its function which precede its creation. You also cannot access a local variable after the function ends as it no longer exists.

Function naming rules are very similar to those of variables:

Cannot use keywords as a function name
Cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or underscore
All other characters must be a letter, number or underscore
Uppercase and lowercase characters are distinct

And like variables, the function name should be descriptive of the task carried out by the function.

title: 5: Functions
text:
Defining a function:
def function_name(parameter_1,parameter_2, ...):
    statement_1
    statement_2
    ...

The function header is the first line of the function and includes the keyword def and the name of the function. This is followed by parentheses where the (optional) parameters needed by the function are placed and then ended with a colon.
Inside the function we have the statement or statements that you want the function to perform. Note that the statements inside the function must be indented.

title: 5: Functions
text:
To use a function, we call it by invoking its name.

def add(x,y):
    print(x + y)

add(2,3)

5


The simple function add above takes in two parameters, x and y then prints their summed value. A parameter is a variable that is assigned the value of an argument when the function is called. We call the function with specific values for the parameters, arguments, in this case 2 and 3 using the notation add(2,3). Note that the function assigns the parameter values in order of the arguments that are passed in. 2 is the first argument, so it is assigned to x and 3 is the second argument so it is assigned to y.
Functions can take in multiple arguments, a single argument or none at all. How many parameters are needed for a function is dependent on its construction.

title: 5: Functions
text:
The function we just saw does not return any data back out of the function, it simply prints a value to the terminal. We call this type of function that executes the statements it contains and then ends a void function.
In contrast, a value-returning function executes its statements and then returns some value back to the point of the program that called it. The input and int functions are example of value-returning functions that you have used.
To return a value from a function, you need only use the return keyword.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

5


We can see in the modified version of our add function that we now return the sum of the values instead of printing to the terminal. This returned value is stored in the result variable and then this variable is printed to the terminal. Note that we do not need to tell Python what type of value is being returned unlike in some other programming languages. The return keyword only specifics to send that value back, there is no check to see what type of value it actually is.


We can return multiple values by separating the values by commas.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

(5, 2, 3)


Our add function now returns the sum, then the value associated with parameter x and finally the value associated with parameter y. Note that the values are returned in the order they are specified. Also note that the variable result is now a tuple containing three objects, which is what we would expect since we returned three individual values.
We can assign these values immediately using the convention for multiple assignment:

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result, x, y = add(2,3)
print(result)
print(x)
print(y)

5
2
3


If you choose to do multiple assignment from a function call, you will need exactly as many variables as there are returned values.



You can use the pass keyword to create empty functions. This keyword is ignored by the Python interpreter and this can be helpful when designing a program.

def a_function():
    pass

title: 5: Functions
text:
Changes made to a parameter value within the function do not affect the argument. This is known as pass by value and it provides a way for unidirectional communication between one function and another function.

def function_1():
    value = 5
    print(f'The value is {value}')
    function_2(value)
    print(f'The value is {value}')

def function_2(x):
    print(f'The value is {x}')
    x = 0
    print(f'The value is now {x}')

A keyword argument is an argument that specifies which parameter the value should be passed to.
function_name(parameter=value)
Note that the position when calling the function is not relevant. It is also possible to mix keyword arguments and positional arguments when calling a function but all positional arguments must appear first.
Keyword arguments are often used to provide a default argument for a parameter. A default argument is a value that will be there by default unless explicitly overwritten when the function is called.

def show_tax(price, tax_rate=0.08):
    tax = price * tax_rate
    print(f'The tax is {tax}.')

show_tax(10)

show_tax(10,tax_rate=0.10)

The tax is 0.8.
The tax is 1.0.

title: 8: Control Structures
text:
Control Structures
A control structure is a logical design that controls the order in which a set of statements executes.
So far, we have been dealing with what is known as a sequence structure, where our set of statements executes in the order they appear. What we will learn now is how to implement decision (or selection) structures, where specific action(s) are performed only if some condition exists.

title: 8: Control Structures
text:
The if Statement
The if statement is the fundamental statement when it comes to creating a decision structure in Python (and in most other languages). It is a single alternative decision. Action(s) are performed should the condition be True and the program continues on the same after the block regardless of state of the condition.
Python syntax:
if condition:

    Statement

    Statement

    ...
The first line is known as the if clause. This is the keyword if followed by the condition that needs to be True for the statement(s) below to be executed. If the condition is False then all the statements inside the block are skipped.

x = 6

if x > 5:
    print(f'The value of x is: {x}')
    print("x is greater than five")

print("Continuing on...")   

The value of x is: 6
x is greater than five
Continuing on...



x = 5

if x > 5:
    print(f'The value of x is: {x}')
    print("x is greater than five")  

print("Continuing on...")   

Continuing on...


Note that the statements must be indented inside the block. If left on the same level, you will have a syntax error, or worse, they will be evaluated after the block ends.

x = 5

if x > 5:
    print(f'The value of x is: {x}')
print("x is greater than five")

print("Continuing on...")   

x is greater than five
Continuing on...


The example above is missing the indent on the second print statement and so what is printed to the console is not reflective of what the value of x actually is.

Single-Line if Statements
An if statement can be written on a single line if it executes only one statement.

score = 70

if score > 60: print('You passed!')

You passed!


Multiple statements require you to use the standard if structure.

title: 8: Control Structures
text:
The if-else Statement
The if-else statement is a dual alternative decision structure. Now, there are two possible paths of execution, one path is taken if the condition is Trueand the second path if the condition is False.
Note that the if clause and else clause must be aligned and that all the statements must be consistently indented.

x = 5

if x > 5:
    print("x is greater than five")
else:
    print("x is not greater than five")

x is not greater than five



Convert the following scenario to Python code.
If the temperature is below 40 degrees, print “It is cold outside.” Otherwise, print “The weather is nice.”


Click to show answer

if temperature < 40:
    print("It is cold outside.")
else:
    print("The weather is nice.")



Conditional Expressions
A conditional expression is a terse way of performing a conditional assignment on a single line.
The general format is:
value_1 if condition else value_2

condition is a Boolean expression that is tested
If condition is True, the expression gives us value_1
If condition is False, the expression gives us value_2

The following conditional expression reads: if score is greater than 59, grade is assigned ‘Pass’. Otherwise, grade is assigned ‘Fail’.

score = 50

grade = 'Pass' if score > 59 else 'Fail'

print(grade)

Fail


Which is equivalent to:

score = 50

if score > 59:
    grade = 'Pass'
else:
    grade = 'Fail'

print(grade)

Fail



Write a conditional expression to assign the larger of two numbers to a variable named “max”.


Click to show answer

title: 8: Control Structures
text:
Nested and Compound Decision Structures
Often we need to test multiple simultaneous conditions.
For example, we need to determine if someone qualifies for a loan and they must meet two conditions:

Must earn at least $30,000/year
Must have been employed for at least two years

We have to approaches here, we can use a compound Boolean expression:
if income >= 30000 and length_employment >= 2:
    print('Qualified')
Where the and operator enforces that both expressions must be True for the overall expression to be True.
Or, we can nest a decision structure inside of another:
if income >= 30000:
    if length_employment >= 2:
        print('Qualified')
We check the first (outer) condition to see if it is True, and if so, we then move inside the first statement and now test the second condition (the inner condition) to see if it is True.
Note that it is very important to use proper indentation in a nested decision structure. It can be easy to write code that is syntax-correct, but logically invalid due to misplaced indentation.

section: Assignment Expressions and the Walrus Operator
text:
Assignment Expressions and the Walrus Operator
The walrus operator := is a combination operator that assigns a value to a variable and returns the value that was assigned to the variable. These are known as assignment expressions.

print(num := 99)

99


This statement does two things:

It assigns 99 to the num variable
It prints the value that was assigned to the num variable, 99

Importantly, num now exists as a variable and can be referred to in future sections of code.
if (area := width * height) > 100:
    print('The area is too large')
This statement does the following:

The area variable is assigned the value of width * height
If the value that was assigned to area is greater than 100, the message The area is too large is displayed.

Note that an assignment expression is not a complete statement. All of our examples used the assignment expression as a component of some other statement. This is a requirement in Python as an assignment expression alone will cause an error:
num := 15
The code above is invalid, and the expression must be written as part of a larger statement like
print(num:= 15)

Precedence of the walrus operator
The walrus operator has the lowest precedence of all the operators in Python. When using the walrus operator in a larger expression that also uses other operators, the walrus operator will work last. In most cases, you need to put parentheses around the assignment expression to make sure the walrus operator assigns the correct value to its variable

title: 3: Strings, Lists and Tuples
text:
Recall that a string is sequence of characters that is one of Python’s fundamental data types.
For example, name = input(“Enter a name”) the variable name is a string.
You might see the term string literal used, which is a string that appears in actual code of a program in contrast to the data type.
In the above example “Enter a name” is a string literal.
Often, the term literal is omitted and the word string is used both for the data type and actual character sequence. It is usually easy enough with context to distinguish between the two.


String concatenation is the process of appending one string to another string.
We can use the + operator to concatenate strings.

message = 'Hello ' + 'world'

print(message)

Hello world


We can use string concatenation to break up a long string literal. This is especially useful if you are writing code on a device with limited screen width.

print('Enter the amount of ' +

'sales for each day and ' +

'press Enter.')

Enter the amount of sales for each day and press Enter.


Notice how this statement is printed all on a single line.



Strings are immutable. Once they are created, they cannot be changed
Under the surface, concatenation does not change the existing string, but rather creates a new string and assigns it to the previously used variable.
As a consequence of immutability, we cannot use an expression of the form: string[index] = new_character . A statement like this that attempts to overwrite a part of the string will result in an error.



An f-string (formatted string literal) is a special type of string literal that is prefixed with the letter f. These are often used to make customization and formatting of the printed output an easier process.

print(f'Hello world')

Hello world


One of the most useful features of f-strings is that they support placeholders for variables.

name = 'Johnny'

print(f'Hello {name}.')

Hello Johnny.


Placeholders can also be expressions that are evaluated.

print(f'The value is {10 + 2}.')

The value is 12.



val = 10

print(f'The value is {val + 2}.')

The value is 12.


Format specifiers can be used to add additional formatting that controls things like the number of decimal places displayed or to what precision a number is rounded.

num = 123.456789

print(f'{num:.2f}')

123.46



2f means:

round the value to 2 decimal places
display the value as a floating-point number

Percentages


discount = 0.5

print(f'{discount:.0%}')

50%



Scientific Notation


num = 12345.6789

print(f'{num:.2e}')

1.23e+04


When using multiple designators in a format specifier, the order is as follows: [alignment][width][,][.precision][type]

Example: print(f'{number:^10,.2f}')

There are many other options and ways of formatting strings in Python. The office reference material at https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html contains extensive details.



Strings in Python have many types of methods, divided into different types of operations.

General format: mystring.method(arguments)

Some methods test a string for specific characteristics. These are generally Boolean methods in that they return True if a condition exists, and False otherwise.









Method
Description




isalnum()
Returns true if the string contains only alphabetic letters or digits and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise.


isalpha()
Returns true if the string contains only alphabetic letters and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise.


isdigit()
Returns true if the string contains only numeric digits and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise.


islower()
Returns true if all of the alphabetic letters in the string are lowercase, and the string contains at least one alphabetic letter. Returns false otherwise.


isspace()
Returns true if the string contains only whitespace characters and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise. (Whitespace characters are spaces, newlines (\n), and tabs (\t).


isupper()
Returns true if all of the alphabetic letters in the string are uppercase, and the string contains at least one alphabetic letter. Returns false otherwise.



Some methods return a copy of the string, to which modifications have been made. These simulate strings as mutable objects.
Note that string comparisons are case-sensitive.

Uppercase characters are distinguished from lowercase characters
lower and upper methods can be used for making case-insensitive string comparisons











Method
Description




lower()
Returns a copy of the string with all alphabetic letters converted to lowercase. Any character that is already lowercase, or is not an alphabetic letter, is unchanged.


lstrip()
Returns a copy of the string with all leading whitespace characters removed. Leading whitespace characters are spaces, newlines (\n), and tabs (\t) that appear at the beginning of the string.


lstrip(char)
The char argument is a string containing a character. Returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the beginning of the string removed.


rstrip()
Returns a copy of the string with all trailing whitespace characters removed. Trailing whitespace characters are spaces, newlines(\n), and tabs (\t) that appear at the end of the string.


rstrip(char)
The char argument is a string containing a character. The method returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the end of the string removed.


strip()
Returns a copy of the string with all leading and trailing whitespace characters removed.


strip(char)
Returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the beginning and the end of the string removed.


upper()
Returns a copy of the string with all alphabetic letters converted to uppercase. Any character that is already uppercase, or is not an alphabetic letter, is unchanged.



Programs commonly need to search for substrings, a smaller component of a string.
There are several methods to accomplish this:










Method
Description




endswith(substring)
The substring argument is a string. The method returns True if the string ends with substring.


find (substring)
The substring argument is a string. The method returns the lowest index in the string where substring is found. If substring is not found, the method returns negative 1


replace(old, new)
The old and new arguments are both strings. The method returns a copy of the string with all instances of old replaced by new.


startswith (substring)
The substring argument is a string. The method returns True if the string starts with substring.







The repetition operator * makes multiple copies of a string and joins them together. This is only applicable when the operands are a string (on the left) and an integer (on the right).
General format: string_to_copy * n
The output references a new string which contains multiple copies of the original string.



Sometimes a string contains substrings that are separated by a special character.

Example: 'peach raspberry strawberry vanilla'

This example contains the substrings peach, raspberry, strawberry, and vanilla if we choose the space to be our separator.
The substrings are separated by the space character and the substrings are known as tokens with separating character being the delimiter

The string '17;92;81;12;46;5' contains the tokens 17, 92, 81, 12, 46, and 5 if we choose the delimiter to be the ; character.

Tokenizing is the process of breaking a string into tokens. When you tokenize a string, you extract the tokens and store them as individual items.
In Python you can use the split method to tokenize a string.


The split method returns a list containing the tokens in the string.
By default, the split method uses the space as separator to define what these tokens are. We can specify a different separator by passing it as an argument to the split method.

str = 'peach raspberry strawberry vanilla'

tokens = str.split()

print(tokens)

['peach', 'raspberry', 'strawberry', 'vanilla']



my_address = 'www.example.com'

tokens = my_address.split('.')

print(tokens)

['www', 'example', 'com']



my_string = '1/2/3/4/5'

number_list = my_string.split('/')

print(number_list)

['1', '2', '3', '4', '5']

isupper()
Returns true if all of the alphabetic letters in the string are uppercase, and the string contains at least one alphabetic letter. Returns false otherwise.



Some methods return a copy of the string, to which modifications have been made. These simulate strings as mutable objects.
Note that string comparisons are case-sensitive.

Uppercase characters are distinguished from lowercase characters
lower and upper methods can be used for making case-insensitive string comparisons











Method
Description

Returns a copy of the string with all alphabetic letters converted to lowercase. Any character that is already lowercase, or is not an alphabetic letter, is unchanged.


lstrip()
Returns a copy of the string with all leading whitespace characters removed. Leading whitespace characters are spaces, newlines (\n), and tabs (\t) that appear at the beginning of the string.


lstrip(char)
The char argument is a string containing a character. Returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the beginning of the string removed.


rstrip()
Returns a copy of the string with all trailing whitespace characters removed. Trailing whitespace characters are spaces, newlines(\n), and tabs (\t) that appear at the end of the string.


rstrip(char)

strip()

strip(char)

upper()
Returns a copy of the string with all alphabetic letters converted to uppercase. Any character that is already uppercase, or is not an alphabetic letter, is unchanged.

Method

t = (10, 20, [97, 98, 99])

title: 16: Distance and Similarity
text:
Distance and the Feature Space
So far, we have viewed vectors as arrows in 2D or 3D physical space. In modern computing, a vector is just a list of features.
If an object has 5 attributes, they can be viewed as a single point in a 5-Dimensional Vector Space. While we cannot draw 5D space, the mathematics work the same. The exact same NumPy addition and dot products we used for 2D apply to 5D or 10,000-dimensional data.
A row in a DataFrame is just a point in a high-dimensional space.
The DataFrame below has a dimension of three, since it contains three features.

import pandas as pd

patients = pd.DataFrame({
    "Age": [45, 48, 52, 51],
    "HeartRate": [72, 75, 68, 77],
    "BloodPressure": [120, 125, 118, 131]
})

We can think of the x-coordinate as age, the y-coordinate as heart rate, and the z-coordinate as blood pressure.


Show Python plotting code
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Age": [45, 48, 52, 51 ],
    "HeartRate": [72, 75, 68, 77],
    "BloodPressure": [120, 125, 118, 131]
})

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7,7))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

ax.scatter(df["Age"], df["HeartRate"], df["BloodPressure"], s=60)

ax.set_xlabel("Age")
ax.set_ylabel("Heart Rate")
ax.set_zlabel("Blood Pressure")

ax.view_init(elev=30, azim=105)

ax.xaxis.pane.fill = False
ax.yaxis.pane.fill = False
ax.zaxis.pane.fill = False

plt.show()









Note that we can switch any of these labels between axes, the specific choice is not important for calculations.
We can also see that every row is one point and every column is one feature.

print(patients.iloc[0])

Age               45
HeartRate         72
BloodPressure    120
Name: 0, dtype: int64

title: 16: Distance and Similarity
section: How Close Are Two Data Points?
text:
How Close Are Two Data Points?
To find similar things, we measure the distance between their vectors. The closer the distance, the more similar the objects are.
The question is, how to calculate the distance?

Distance Measures
There are many ways to calculate the distance in a vector space.
We will talk about the two most commonly used methods.

Euclidean Distance (Straight-line Distance)
Manhattan Distance (City Block Distance)



Euclidean Distance (Straight-line Distance)
Euclidean distance is defined as
D_E(x,y) = \sqrt{(x_1 - y_1)^2 + (x_2 - y_2)^2 + ... + (x_n - y_n)^2}
and is used for measurements that are numerical and continuous.
Note that this is just an application of familiar Pythagorean theorem.

# Two patients: [Age, Heart_Rate, Blood_Pressure]
import numpy as np

patient_A = np.array([45, 72, 120])
patient_B = np.array([48, 75, 125])

# Calculate the distance vector, then take its norm

distance = np.linalg.norm(patient_A - patient_B)



Manhattan Distance (City Block Distance)
Sometimes a straight line is impossible or gives too much weight to certain large differences. Manhattan distance can then be used, which is the sum of the absolute differences.
D_M(x,y) = |x_1 - y_1| + |x_2 - y_2| + ... + |x_n - y_n|

# Two patients: [Age, Heart_Rate, Blood_Pressure]

patient_A = np.array([45, 72, 120])
patient_B = np.array([48, 75, 125])

distance = np.linalg.norm(patient_A - patient_B, ord=1)



Finding the Closest Match
How does a computer classify something new?

It finds the closest historical data point.

We will develop an algorithm to find the closest match in our DataFrame for a given point.

We need to iterate through every row in the DataFrame, as we will not know if there is a closer pair unless we examine every pair.
We then need to calculate the distance between each pair.
We will need to keep track of the smallest distance.


best_distance = infinity
for every row:
compute distance
if smaller:
remember row

Try converting the pseudocode above before looking at this solution.


Show Solution
unknown = np.array([46,74,121])
smallest_distance = np.inf

for _, row in df.iterrows():
    d = np.linalg.norm(row.to_numpy() - unknown)

    if d < smallest_distance:
        smallest_distance = d

print(smallest_distance)


2.449489742783178



We can find the same answer by using the min() method if we calculate all the distances beforehand. One of the benefits of arrays in NumPy is the ability to perform operations on every object in the array.

unknown = np.array([46,74,121])

distances = np.linalg.norm( patients.to_numpy() - unknown,
                            axis=1 #this specifies we calculate across the columns
                          )
print(distances.min())

2.449489742783178


What about finding the two closest points?
Most of our code can be reused, but we will need to keep track of the second smallest distance.

Try developing this on your own using the solution to the single closest point.


Show Solution
smallest_distance, second_smallest_distance = np.inf, np.inf

for _, row in patients.iterrows():
    d = np.linalg.norm(row.to_numpy() - unknown)

    if d < smallest_distance:
        second_smallest_distance = smallest_distance
        smallest_distance = d

    elif d < second_smallest_distance:
        second_smallest_distance = d



What about finding the three closest points?
We now need to have conditions that handle:

the observation is the smallest overall
the observation is the second smallest overall
the observation is the third smallest overall

We need a better solution than continuing to create conditional statements. What we can do is collect all the distances in a list, then sort the list.

unknown = np.array([46,74,121])

distances = []

for _, row in patients.iterrows():
    d = np.linalg.norm(row.to_numpy() - unknown)
    distances.append(d)

distances.sort()

print(distances)

[np.float64(2.449489742783178), np.float64(4.58257569495584), np.float64(9.0), np.float64(11.575836902790225)]


Again, we can simply the code needed by leveraging the capability in NumPy to operate across an entire array.

distances = np.linalg.norm( df.to_numpy() - unknown,
                            axis=1 #this specifies we calculate across the columns
                            )

distances = np.sort(distances)

print(distances)

[ 2.44948974  4.58257569  9.         11.5758369 ]




Not Every Feature Needs to Count Equally
Suppose we have two data points with the following features:

Age = 45 and Income = $900,000
Age = 46 and Income = $901,000

In terms of raw numbers, income dominates because the units are much larger.
Does a difference of $1,000 matter more than a year of age? It depends, but this is is why we often rescale data before measuring distance. This is outside of the scope of this course but is important in applications.


Distance is everywhere.
Finding similar customers, movie recommendations, fraud detection, facial recognition, spell checking are all calculating distances. Most of “AI” involves measuring distance as a core component. If you can turn it into a vector, you can measure distance.

Images as Vectors
For example, we can represent images as vectors fairly easily. Each image exists in two dimensions and we need some value to indicate the color or intensity. So something like a 3-tuple x, y, i can be used to specify an individual pixel value.
But a more convenient representation from a programming perspective is to flatten these values down into a single vector. If we keep a consistent way of ordering the values in the vector, then this directly corresponds to the pixel location and we only need to keep track of the intensity.
The image below holds a (fairly crude) version of the number seven. We then can transform it into a flattened vector simply by merging all the individual arrays into one large array.

title: 16: Distance and Similarity
text:
Direction and Magnitude
Looking at the plot we can see that vector A points in the same direction as vector B. But vectors A and C are much closer according to Euclidean distance.


Show Python plotting code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

A = np.array([1,1])
B = np.array([4,4])
C = np.array([-1,1])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,6))

colors = {'A':'red', 
          'B':'blue',
          'C':'green'}

for vec, label in zip([B,A,C],["B", "A", "C"]):
    ax.quiver(
        0,0,
        vec[0],vec[1],
        angles='xy',
        scale_units='xy',
        scale=1,
        width=0.008,
        color=colors[label]
        
    )
    ax.text(vec[0]-0.5, vec[1]-0.0, label, fontsize=22)

ax.set_xlim(-2,5)
ax.set_ylim(-1,5)

ax.grid(True)
ax.set_aspect("equal")

plt.show()










A = np.array([1,1])
B = np.array([4,4])
C = np.array([-1,1])

print(f'A - B = {np.linalg.norm(A - B)}')
print(f'A - C = {np.linalg.norm(A - C)}')

A - B = 4.242640687119285
A - C = 2.0


Changing to Manhattan distance, we see that A and B are even further apart than Euclidean.

print(f'A - B = {np.linalg.norm((A - B), ord = 1)}')
print(f'A - C = {np.linalg.norm((A - C), ord = 1)}')

A - B = 6.0
A - C = 2.0


A better way to approach this is to avoid distance and instead look at the angle between the two vectors. The closer the angle is to zero, the more the vectors point in the same direction. So, the closer the angle to zero, the more similar the vectors are.


Show Python plotting code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,6))
ax.quiver(0,0,A[0],A[1],
          angles='xy',scale_units='xy',scale=1)

ax.quiver(0,0,B[0],B[1],
          angles='xy',scale_units='xy',scale=1)

ax.plot([A[0],B[0]],
        [A[1],B[1]],
        linewidth=3)

ax.scatter(*A,s=100)
ax.scatter(*B,s=100)

ax.text(2.5,2.7,"Large Euclidean\nDistance",
        ha='right',
        bbox=dict(facecolor='white'))

ax.set_xlim(0,5)
ax.set_ylim(0,5)

ax.grid(True)
ax.set_aspect("equal")

plt.show()










The Dot Product
Recall that the dot product (scalar product) measures how much one vector is aligned in the direction of another.
This is best seen with the definition that uses the lengths of the vectors and the cosine of the angle between them:
u \cdot v = |u| |v| \cos{\theta}


Cosine Similarity
From this form of the dot product definition, we can simultaneously find the angle between the vectors and translate it to a convenient range.


Show Python plotting code
theta = np.linspace(-0.5,0.5,100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,6))

ax.quiver(0,0,A[0],A[1],
          angles='xy',scale_units='xy',scale=1,color='red')

ax.quiver(0,0,C[0],C[1],
          angles='xy',scale_units='xy',scale=1,color='green')

ax.plot(
    [-0.5,0.5],
    [0.5,0.5],
    linewidth=3
)

ax.text(-0.05,0.20,r"$\theta$",
        fontsize=18)

ax.set_xlim(-2,2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5,2)

ax.grid(True)
ax.set_aspect("equal")

plt.show()









By a simple rearrangement of the dot product definition we have:
\cos(\theta) = \frac{u \cdot v}{|u||v|}
With our cosine similarity definition, we can now calculate the similarity between two vectors in a way that ignores differences in magnitude and considers only direction.
Looking at our original vectors, we see that the results of cosine similarity are better matched to our intuition of how far the vectors are apart.

def similarity(A,B):
    return np.dot(A,B) / (np.linalg.norm(A) * np.linalg.norm(B))

A = np.array([1,1])
B = np.array([4,4])
C = np.array([-1,1])

print(f'Cosine similarity between A and B: {similarity(A, B)}\n')

print(f'Cosine similarity between A and C: {similarity(A, C)}')

Cosine similarity between A and B: 0.9999999999999998

Cosine similarity between A and C: 0.0


Note that a cosine similarity of -1 means the two vectors are closely related, they are just in opposite directions.
If we had vectors of words, good and bad are related words, one is the opposite of the other.

These would likely have a cosine similarity of -1.




Cosine Similarity
Meaning




1
Same direction


0.8
Very similar


0
Unrelated directions


-1
Opposite directions

As these words are unrelated, we would expect a cosine similarity around zero.

Meaning

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Lists and Vectors
Standard Python is designed for general software development, not math. Structures like lists in Python have their own set of rules that makes using them in mathematical operations difficult. If we try to perform math on a standard Python list, the results are either completely wrong for our purposes, or they crash the program.
Consider a list of test scores: scores = [85, 90, 78]
If we want to double the score of every student, our first instinct is to multiply the list by 2:

print(scores * 2)

But what happens is it repeats the list items

scores = [85, 90,  78]
print(scores * 2)

[85, 90, 78, 85, 90, 78]


Now, if we try to add 2 bonus points to every score using scores + 2, Python throws a TypeError because it does not understand how to combine a list with an integer.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Libraries

If we want mathematics to play well with the idea of lists, we need more specialized tools.
Libraries are external toolsets built that we can bring into our Python code.
For numerical data, the industry standard is NumPy (Numerical Python).
If you are working on a local machine, you likely need to install the library first using pip install numpy in your terminal.
Cloud environments like Colab usually have it pre-installed.


Standard Library Functions and the import Statement

Standard library: library of pre-written functions that comes with Python

Library functions perform tasks that programmers commonly need

Example: print, input, range
Viewed by programmers as a “black box”


Some library functions built into Python interpreter

To use, just call the function

Modules: files that stores functions of the standard library

Help organize library functions not built into the interpreter
Copied to computer when you install Python

To call a function stored in a module, need to write an import statement

Written at the top of the program
Format: import module_name




Importing NumPy

Once you have access to NumPy we need to use an import statement:


import numpy as np


We use as np as a standard convention.
It acts as a nickname so we do not have to type “numpy” every time we want to use one of its tools.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Creating Arrays

To use NumPy’s features, we must convert our standard Python list into a specialized NumPy object called a ndarray (n-dimensional array).


scores = [85, 90, 78]

np_scores = np.array(scores)


Our data is now stored in a format designed for mathematics.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Vectorization

Vectorization allows operations to be applied to every element in the array at the exact same time.
We can now multiply our collection by two and get the result that we initially anticipated.


print(np_scores * 2)

[170 180 156]

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Comparison Between Arrays and Lists

Standard Python List:

Designed to store mixed data types natively.
Mathematical operators like + concatenate and * repeat.
Can hold mixed types like [1, "apple", True].

NumPy ndarray:

Designed for math.
Must hold uniform data types.

Warning: If you put a string into an array of numbers NumPy will silently convert your numbers into strings to maintain uniformity.

arr = np.array([85, 90, "apple"])
print(arr)

['85' '90' 'apple']

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Scalars

The standard textbook definition of a scalar is “a quantity with magnitude but no direction.”
Another more useful definition when it comes to dealing with vectors is a scalar is a scaling factor.

It is a quantity that stretches or shrinks something else.

In Python: A scalar is a standard integer or float like x = 5.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Vectors
A vector is an ordered list of coordinates that gives us instructions on how to move through space. The dimensionality of the space is the number of values in the vector.
In math, v = [3, 2] means “start at the origin, go 3 units along the x-axis and 2 units along y-axis.” The vector v here has two elements and so the space the vector is in is 2-dimensional.
We can represent this in Python as a 1-dimensional NumPy array.

import numpy as np

v = np.array([3, 2])


Visually, we have:

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Vector Arithmetic

Magnitude
The magnitude of a vector is its length.
We can find the magnitude of a vector v = [a, b, c, ...] by using the Euclidean distance |v| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + ...}
From the definition of the magnitude we can see that it is always non-negative and is a scalar value.


Example

Assume you walk 3m east then 4m north.
We can find the straight-line distance from your starting point to your destination using the magnitude of the sum of the vectors.
Since we are working in a 2-dimensional space this is just the Pythagorean theorem.


east= np.array([3,0])

north = np.array([0,4])

np.linalg.norm(east+north)

np.float64(5.0)




Addition and Subtraction
Adding (or subtracting) two vectors is combining their instructions.
This can be visualized with the “head to tail” method.


a = np.array([2, 1])

b = np.array([1, 3])

print(a + b)

[3 4]




Scalar Multiplication
Applying a positive scalar to a vector scales its magnitude (length) without changing its fundamental line of direction.
Applying a negative scalar scales its magnitude and changes the direction exactly 180 degrees.


v = np.array([3, 4])

print(2 * v)

[6 8]


Note that the vector in the code about is twice as long when scaled by 2.


Vector Multiplication
It is natural to assume that if you can do a + b then you can do a \times b. However, when it comes to vectors simply placing an \times between them is undefined. We need to specify exactly what we are calculating.
There are in fact three different ways to “multiply” vectors. These are not different ways to do the same thing, they are entirely different tools design to answer entirely different questions.


The Hadamard Product
In NumPy, the * operator is defined for vectors. That is, a * b will result in output. But it is not likely to be the output you wanted.

a = np.array([1, 2])

b = np.array([3, 4])

print(a * b)

[3 8]


This is the Hadamard product, which is used to scale the corresponding components of two vectors independently. The Hadamard product simply multiples matching elements:
[a,b] * [c,d] = [a*c, b*d]
That is, it performs element-wise multiplication.
Note that the output is a vector of the same dimensions as the inputs.
The Hadamard product is not often used because it depends on the coordinate system chosen (a choice which is often changed due to mathematical convenience).


The Dot Product
The dot product (or scalar product) is used to determine how much two vectors point in the same direction.
The dot product has two formulations (where |v| is the magnitude of the vector v)
a \cdot b = |a||b|\cos(\theta )
a \cdot b = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + ...
Note that the output of the dot product is a scalar (hence the term scalar product).

a = np.array([1, 2])

b = np.array([3, 4])

print(np.dot(a, b)) # print(a @ b) is equivalent

11


We can use the dot product to determine the projection of one vector onto another. Note that orthogonal (perpendicular) vectors have a dot product of zero.

We will use the dot product later in the course as it can be used to calculate the similarity between two objects that have a vector representation.


The Cross Product
The cross product finds the unique direction that is perpendicular to both of the vectors and its associated magnitude.
The output of the cross product is a vector itself.

This implies that we need at least a 3-dimensional space to work in.

If we take two vectors, they form a flat 2D pane. The cross product produces a new vector completely out of that pane, perpendicular to both.

The length (magnitude) of this new vector represents the area of the parallelogram formed by the original two vectors.

If the two vectors point in the exact same direction, their cross product is zero (no area, no leverage).
If they are perpendicular, the cross product is at its maximum.


a = np.array([4, 1, 0])

b = np.array([1, 4, 0])

# The cross product

print(np.cross(a, b))

[ 0  0 15]

Attributes in NumPy
Arrays in NumPy have certain inherent properties, called attributes, that can be useful for diagnosing errors or just inspecting the array. Note that attributes are different from functions, so they do not use parentheses () at the end.

array.shape
array.shape returns a tuple indicating the number of elements along each axis.

For a 1D array it returns (n,).
For a 2D array it returns (number of rows, number of columns).

Many operations involving vectors require equivalent shapes. For example, the dot product is defined only on two vectors of identical length. array.shape can be used to help diagnose or prevent errors like this.

prices = np.array([10, 20, 30])

print(prices.shape)# Output: (3,) A 1D array with 3 elements

grid = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])

print(grid.shape)# Output: (3, 2) 3 rows, 2 columns

(3,)
(3, 2)


Note that the comma in a 1D shape like (3,) is because Python handles tuples with a trailing comma to distinguish them from regular parentheses.

It means “3 elements in the first dimension, and no other dimensions exist.”



array.ndim
array.ndim returns the total number of dimensions (axes) that the array has.

A scalar has ndim = 0
A vector has ndim = 1
A matrix has ndim = 2



array.dtype
array.dtype tells you exactly what kind of data is stored inside.
This can be very useful as NumPy enforces uniform types. If a single string slips into your numbers, the whole array converts to text. Checking .dtype reveals if your numbers have become strings.

Average: Takes the arithmetic mean of the array.

np.mean()

np.sum()

np.max()

Min: Returns the smallest element in the array.

np.min()




Reshape
array.reshape() changes the dimensions of an array without changing its actual data.

flat_data = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])

# Morph it into 3 rows and 2 columns

grid_data = flat_data.reshape(3, 2)

print(grid_data)

[[1 2]
 [3 4]

Note that you cannot reshape an array into dimensions that do not fit the number of elements.
If you try flat_data.reshape(3, 3) on the above array, NumPy will throw a: ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 6 into shape (3,3). The shape (3,3) requires exactly 9 items, and we only have 6.


Flatten
array.flatten() takes a multi-dimensional grid and squashes it back down into a single 1D row. This iu Useful when a library expects a flat sequence of values, but you currently have them inside a multi-dimensional structure.

grid_data = np.array([[1, 2],[3, 4],[5, 6]])

If you run np.mean(scores)and the result is just NaN, having just a single broken data point has ruined your calculation. Combining this with an aggregate tool allows you to count how many broken points you have.

[False  True False]
1

title: 6: Basic Plotting
text:
The matplotlib package is a library for creating two-dimensional charts and graphs. Like NumPy, it is not part of the standard Python library, so you will have to install it separately.
The matplotlib package contains a module named pyplot that you will need to import. Use the following import statement to import the module and create an alias named plt:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Plotting in matplotlib is no different conceptually than using x, y coordinates on graph paper.
If you give matplotlib an array of X data points and an array of X data points, it pairs them up sequentially: (𝑥_0, 𝑦_0 ), (𝑥_1, 𝑦_1 ), … and draws a line between them.


To plot data, we first need some.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
y = x ** 2



Before we draw anything, we have to set up our canvas. In Matplotlib, this is done using the Object-Oriented API, which separates the window from the chart itself.
-The Figure (fig): The blank canvas that the plots will be drawn on. It controls global settings like size, background color, and layout. -The Axes (ax): The specific plot inside the figure. This contains the actual x and y axes, tick marks, labels, titles, and the data lines.
Note that there is a substantial number of examples that use the older plt.plot() style, which blends these two concepts together and requires one less line of code. While slightly faster for simple plots, it is much easier to use the figure and axis architecture when you want to customize things.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.show()








We can see that we get a completely blank set of axes of 6 inches in width and 4 inches in height.
It is very important to avoid forgetting plt.show(). If you write all your ax.plot() code but forget plt.show() at the very end, Python will just silently finish running and show you nothing.
We now need to actually apply content to the axes to see our plot. We will use use ax.plot(x, y) to create a line plot.

ax.plot(x, y) 







A line plot is good for shwoing tends over time, distance, area, etc.

days = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
stock_price = np.array([150, 152, 149, 155, 158])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, stock_price) # .plot() defaults to a line
plt.show()











Bar charts are suited for categorical comparisons.

products = np.array(["Software", "Hardware", "Consulting"])
revenue = np.array([50000, 35000, 20000])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(products, revenue)
plt.show()











Scatter plots are useful for seeing if two variables are correlated.

marketing_spend = np.array([1000, 2500, 1500, 4000, 3000])
new_customers = np.array([10, 22, 14, 45, 32])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(marketing_spend, new_customers)
plt.show()












All of our previous plots are incomplete, as there is no context for what the visuals mean.

ax.set_title()

Sets the overall plot title.

ax.set_xlabel()

Sets the title for the x-axis.

ax.set_ylabel()

Sets the title for the y-axis.

ax.legend()

Enables the legend. You need to attach labels to the data form them to be displayed in the legend.


Adding context makes this scatter plot comprehensible.

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(marketing_spend, new_customers)
ax.set_title("Marketing Spend vs. New Customers")
ax.set_xlabel("New Customers")
ax.set_ylabel("Marketing Spend (1000$)")
plt.show()








Whenever we use methods like ax.set_title()or ax.set_xlabel(), we can pass optional arguments to change how the text looks.

fontsize : Accepts an integer representing the point size (e.g., 14), or relative text strings like ‘small’, ‘medium’, ‘large’.
fontweight : Sets the thickness of the font.

Most common choices are ‘normal’, ‘bold’, or ‘light’.

color: Changes the text color.

Matplotlib accepts standard names (‘red’, ‘black’), hexadecimal strings (‘#1e3a8a’), or grayscale floats (‘0.5’).

fontname : Allows changing the font family (e.g., ‘serif’, ‘sans-serif’).

These arguments go directly inside the plotting call itself (like ax.plot(), ax.scatter()). They change how the visual representation of the data is drawn.

color : The color of the line, markers, or bars.
linewidth : The thickness of a line plot (e.g., lw=2.5).
linestyle : The pattern of the line.

Common values are:

‘-’ (solid line)
‘–’ (dashed line)
‘:’ (dotted line)


alpha: Sets the transparency of the element.

It ranges from 0.0 (completely invisible) to 1.0 (completely opaque).
This is very useful when plotting overlapping datasets.

label: The name string associated with this specific data line.

This is what Matplotlib reads automatically when you call ax.legend().


There are many more options than what is listed here that can be found in the offical documentation.
This example combines many of these methods to make a plot that is easy to comprehend.

# Generate data
#linspace here creates a vector of 100 data points evenly spaced from 0 to 10 (inclusive).
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y1 = np.sin(x)
y2 = np.cos(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

# Apply geometric styling to the data presentation

ax.plot(x, y1, color='blue', linestyle='-', linewidth=2, label='Sensor Alpha')
ax.plot(x, y2, color='darkorange', linestyle=':', linewidth=2.5, label='Sensor Beta')

# Apply text styling
# pad creates whitespace between the title text and the plot grid. 
ax.set_title("Sensor Comparison Analysis", fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', pad=15)
ax.set_xlabel("Duration (seconds)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_ylabel("Signal Strength (mV)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

#Styling the legend text and grid line structures

ax.legend(fontsize=11, loc='lower left')
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.4, color='gray')
