section: An Everyday Example of an Object
text:
An Everyday Example of an Object
Consider the idea of a clock.
When it comes to defining the state of our clock its data attributes would be things like second, minute, hour, day, month, etc.
We need the ability to manipulate the object, and so we will need methods to do so. The question is, which methods should be accessible to outside code (public methods) and which should be exclusive to the object’s internal workings (private methods)?
Public methods would be common tasks that someone could expect to do to use the clock, like setting the time, setting the date, creating an alarm, etc.
Private methods would be things like how exactly the alarm functions to produce the sound at the correct time. This is not something one needs to know to use the clock, so it would be best off as a private method.

title: 15: Objects and Classes
text:
Classes
If we have an idea that we can represent as an object, we can specify a blueprint for it. This is a class, which is a collection of specific data attributes and methods for a particular type of object.
When using a class to create an object, we call the created version an instance of the class. The process of creating the object associated with a specific class is called instantiation. Since a class is designed to be a blueprint for an object that will be used repeatedly, then it is reasonable to expect that there can be many instances of one class at the same time. This is a true assumption, and Python differentiates different instances of a class by their memory location.

Class Definitions
To create a class, we need to define it. A class definition is a set of statements that define a class’s methods and data attributes.
Defining a class is similar to defining a function, we need the appropriate keyword class and the name of the class (by convention this starts with an uppercase letter).

To use initial parameters and define methods we need to use the self parameter. This is a special reference to the specific instance of the class.

class Clock:
    
    def __init__(self, seconds, minutes, hours):
        self.seconds = seconds
        self.minutes = minutes
        self.hours = hours

We can see a special initializer method, the constructor for the class. This takes in a single required parameter, self, and for our example, three other parameters passed in during instantiation of the class to the data attributes associated with our specific instance of the class Clock.
This initializer method is automatically executed when an instance of the class is created and is usually the very first method in a class definition.
Consider the following class designed to simulate a coin and the ability to toss it. Note that each method in the class has the self parameter.

import random

class Coin:

    def __init__(self):
        self.sideup = 'Heads'
    
    def toss(self):
        if random.randint(0, 1) == 0:
            self.sideup = 'Heads'
        else:
            self.sideup = 'Tails'
        
    def get_sideup(self):
        return self.sideup

To create a new instance of a class we use the format variable_name = ClassName().

my_coin = Coin()

To call any of the class methods using the created instance we use the dot notation like my_instance.method(). Because the self parameter references the specific instance of the object, the method will affect this instance.

print(my_coin.get_sideup())

Heads



my_coin.toss()
print(my_coin.get_sideup())

Tails


Note that we do not pass in self as an argument. It is implicit in the structure of the method definition. It needs to be there, but we do not need to concern ourselves with it when using the class.


Hiding Attributes and Methods
A key idea in object oriented programming is that certain components of an object data should be private.
In Python, this is indicated by placing two underscores (__) in front of an attribute name or a method definition.
This is our coin class redesigned to better indicate that the data attributes should not be accessed directly from outside the class.

import random

class Coin:

    def __init__(self):
        self.__sideup = 'Heads'
    
    def toss(self):
        if random.randint(0, 1) == 0:
            self.__sideup = 'Heads'
        else:
            self.__sideup = 'Tails'
        
    def get_sideup(self):
        return self.__sideup

Note that we did not apply the double underscores to the toss() and get_sideup() methods. That is because these are designed to be used outside of the class. That is, they are the expected way of interacting with the data attribute __sideup .


Accessor and Mutator Methods
Typically, all of a class’s data attributes are private and provide methods to access and change them. This is a safer way for code outside the class to retrieve or edit the value of attributes.
Accessor methods return a value from a class’s attribute without changing it. In our above example, the get_sideup() method is an accessor.
Mutator methods store or change the value of a data attribute. In our above example, the toss() method is a mutator.
Note that class methods can have multiple parameters in addition to self. This is common with mutator methods where we need to provide the new value of an attribute. We also saw this with the initalizer for our Clock class, it took in three different parameters apart from self.


Passing Objects as Arguments
Methods and functions often need to accept objects as arguments. When you pass an object as an argument, you are actually passing a reference to the object. The receiving method or function has access to the actual object Methods of the object can be called within the receiving function or method, and data attributes may be changed using mutator methods.


Identifying a Class’s Responsibilities
When it comes to creating a class, a good first step is thinking about what the responsibilities of the class are.
A classes responsibilities are:

The things the class is responsible for knowing which helps identify the class’s data attributes.
The actions the class is responsible for doing which helps identify the class’s methods.

To find out a class’s responsibilities look at the problem domain and deduce required information and actions.


Storing Classes in Modules
Classes can be stored in modules for future use using the import statement.
The rules for doing so are simple and similar to that of variable naming conventions. Additionally, the filename for the module must end in .py

We can change the state of an object by making an assignment to one of its instance variables.
Consider the fraction class seen in 18.1 of our text.

class Fraction:

    def __init__(self, top, bottom):
        self.num = top # the numerator is on top

myfraction = Fraction(3, 4)
print(myfraction)

3

4

Mutability
We can change the state of an object by making an assignment to one of its instance variables. For example, we could change the numerator of the fraction by assigning a new value to self.num. Likewise, we could do the same thing for self.den.
These methods are mutators because they mutate or change the internal state of our Fraction object.

text:
Sameness
If two Fraction objects are the same, what does that actually mean?

Do they represent the same number?
Are they both the same object?

We can use the is operator to find out if two references refer to the same object.

myfraction = Fraction(3, 4)
yourfraction = Fraction(3, 4)

print(myfraction is yourfraction)

False



ourfraction = myfraction

print(myfraction is ourfraction)

True


Even though myfraction and yourfraction refer to the same rational number, they are not the same object. If we assign myfraction to ourfraction, then the two variables are aliases of the same object.

text:
Shallow Equality
This type of equality is called shallow equality because it compares only the references (i.e., the memory locations), not the contents of the objects.
Using the == operator to check equality between two user defined objects will return the shallow equality result. In other words, the Fraction objects are equal (==) if they are the same object.

title: 15: Objects and Classes
text:
Deep Equality
We could define equality to mean the fractions are the same in that they represent the same rational number. This type of equality is known as deep equality since it compares the values “deep” in the object, not just the reference to the object.
If two variables refer to the same object, they have both shallow and deep equality.

Composition vs. Inheritance
We have seen two ways for a class to reuse code in another class. But hen do you use inheritance, and when is composition the better choice?
Composition, in general, is usually a better choice than inheritance to reuse code. Inheritance is appropriate when the proposed child class (the one reusing the functionality in its parent) represents a specialization of its parent. That is, class A is a specialization of class B if class A represents a specific type of class B. title: 2: Variables, Arithmetic and Basic I/O
text:
A variable is a name that represents a value stored in memory. Variables are used to access and manipulate data stored in these memory locations.


An assignment is the process that is used to create a variable and make it reference data (or reference different data if the variable already exists).
The general format of an assignment statement is:

The general format for assignment is:
variable_name = expression

For example:

mass = 50

This sets the variable mass to the value 50.
Be careful not to confuse the assignment operator = with the equals sign. In Python, this symbol is used for assignment. When we reach conditional statements in the future, we will see that the equality operator (which asks the questions are two objects equal) is the double equals sign ==.
Note that in our examples, the variable receiving the value is always on the left side. This is a general rule in Python, the variable that takes on the value must be on the left.
We also can only use a variable if there is a value actually assigned to it.
number = 
The code above here is broken, as the variable named number is not assigned to anything. This will cause a syntax error.


You can also assign values to multiple variables in a single statement. This is known as multiple assignment.
The following code blocks are functionally equivalent:

x, y, z = 0, 1, 2


x = 0
y = 1
z = 2





The purpose of data types is to categorize the value located in memory.
The major types in Python are:

int for integer
float for a real number
str for sequences of characters called strings

These can be any kind of symbol from letters to numbers to punctuation and more

bool for Boolean values (True or False)

Some operations behave differently depending on the data type (or may not even be defined at all). For example, the + operator performs standard addition when used on integers and floats but instead performs concatenation when used with two strings.



This example demonstrates the idea of copying by value.

x = 7
y = x
x = 10
print(y)

7



y gets the value of x at the time of assignment
Changing x later does not change y
y still prints 7

For simple data types (numbers, strings, Booleans), assignment behaves like copying a value.
With more complex data types (like lists which will be introduced soon), variables behave differently.
The assignment shares access to the same data. The variable names point to a location that holds a single instance of the data. If you change the data through one variable, it will be reflected to all the other variables that point at the same underlying data.

For simple types (int, float, str, bool) assignment copies the value.
For complex types (lists and many others which will be seen in the future) assignment shares access to the same data.




Python has a set of rules for naming variables. Most of these if ignored will result in a syntax error.

Variable name cannot be a Python keyword
Variable name cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or an underscore
After first character may use letters, digits, or underscores
Variable names are case sensitive

In general, a variable’s name should reflect its use. This makes finding and fixing problems in your code much easier. Note that it is common for certain variables to have very simple names (i, j, k, etc.) when they are used for certain common operations. When starting out, you may want to use a more descriptive name to help your understanding.



We know that variables can reference different values while program is running. This is another way of saying we can reassign variables.
Howver, Python does not check to see if your variable’s type is valid for what you are trying to do (this differs from some other programming languages). If you reassign a variable to a different type, you could break code that was previously working.
Also, in Python, you do not need to worry about deleting variables after they have been used (like some other programming languages). Values that are no longer referenced by variables are automatically removed by Python’s garbage collector.



Casting is the process of converting on type of data to another. In Python this is accomplished by a set of functions that is built directly into the language.









Function
Description
Example
Output




int()
Converts to an integer. Truncates floats towards zero.
int(3.8)int(“4”)
34

Converts to a floating-point number.

33.14


str()
Converts almost any object into its string representation.
str(100)
“100”

Converts to a boolean (True or False).

There are certain restrictions on casting in Python that will cause a runtime error if ignored.

Non-Numeric Strings to Numeric Types

Attempting to cast a string that does not look like a number will raise a ValueError.

int("apple")


Casting Float-like Strings to Integers

Python cannot directly cast a string containing a decimal point straight into an integer.

score = int("98.6")






A magic number is an unexplained numeric value that appears in a program’s code.
For example:
amount = balance * 0.065
The value 0.065 is not specified as to what it actually is. It could be an interest rate, or a fee percentage, or many other possible things. Only the person who wrote the code knows for sure (assuming they remember).
If a magic number is used in many places in a program it can take substantial effort to find and change the number in each location. You take the risk of making a mistake each type you type the magic number the program’s code. This can be the source of difficult to find and frustrating errors.


Rather than using magic numbers, you should used a variable whose purpose is to represent the value. This variable is not intended to be changed during the program and so is called a constant. In practice, Python will allow you to change the value, so it is important to remember that this variable is supposed to be static. The common convention in Python is to use all caps to indicate a constant variable.

INTEREST_RATE = 0.051





None is a special Python value that represents no value assigned yet. Note that None is a value (not an error). Its data type is a unique NoneType.
None is used as a placeholder when a value is unknown or not available.
None is not the same as:

0 (a number)
"" (an empty string)
False (a Boolean)

We use None to:

Initialize a variable before it has a real value
Represent missing or unknown information
Indicate that a result has not been computed yet

Rule to remember: Do not perform math or string operations on None. Any of these operations causes an error.

text:
The print Function
We have already seen the print function in the Hello World example. The print function will be one of the most commonly used functions throughout this course. It is extremely useful when trying to debug code, as you can see the contents of variables as your program progresses through its instructions.

Program Execution Order
In general, statements execute in the order that they appear. Specifically, the go from top (first) to bottom (last). In the future we will see ways of repeating or skipping sections of code.
The output of the following example is ‘one’ then ‘two’ then ‘three’.

print('one')
print('two')
print('three')

one
two
three




Displaying Multiple Items with the Print Function
Python allows one to display multiple items with a single call to print.

Items are separated by commas when passed as arguments.
Arguments displayed in the order they are passed to the function.
Items are automatically separated by a space when displayed on screen.


print('one', 'two', 'three')

one two three


Based off the previous examples we can see that successive print statements place their value(s) on different lines. This is because the print function puts a newline character at the end of printed data. We can change this default newline to a value of our choice using the special argument end.
The following example changes the default newline to a space.

print('one',end=' ')
print('two',end=' ')
print('three',end=' ')

one two three 


Similarly, for multiple items displayed on the same line, we can use the separator argument sep to change the default space to something else.
The following example changes the default space to a dash.

print('one', 'two', 'three',sep='-')

one-two-three


Both of these options can be useful to help format printed values to make reading their output easier.


Newlines and Tabs
Certain special characters are preceded by a backslash \.
These characters are treated as commands inside a string.
To create a newline, we use the character \n.
Note the extra new line in the following example.

print('Hello world\n')
print('Hello world')

Hello world

Hello world


To create a tab, we use \t.
Note the increased whitespace (the tab character) between the words Hello and world.

print('Hello\tworld')

Hello   world


We can also see that there is no additional space here in the string Hello\tworld and yet the tab is still correctly placed. If we included space between the tab and the other parts of the string like:

print('Hello \t world')

Hello    world


We see that there is additional space in the printed output. This is an important feature of printing strings in that anything inside the string is printed exactly as it is written. By adding the spaces to make things easier for us to read inside the string, we altered the output.

The input Function
Many programs need to read input from the user. While many kinds of data can be used as input, we will largely be dealing with the simple input function and working with text data. More complicated kinds of input tend to require more effort to both read and process, so we will avoid these in an introductory course.
The input function displays an optional prompt and then reads input from the keyboard.

variable_name = input("Your Prompt Here")

Note that the input function always returns the data as a string. The prompt is typically a string instructing user to enter a value.
Note that the input function also does not automatically display a space after the prompt.
For example:
name = input("What is your name?  ")
The above does the following:

Displays the string ‘What is your name?’
Reads input, as a string, from the keyboard
Assigns the string that was read from the keyboard to the name variable


Reading Numbers with the input Function
Since the input function always returns a string, if we want to use the input as a number in calculations we will need to cast the string to the appropriate numerical type.
number = int(input('Enter a number: '))
The above does the following:

Displays the string ‘Enter a number:’
Reads input, as a string, from the keyboard
Converts the input to an int
Assigns the resulting int to the number variable

Using the range Function With the for Loop
The range function returns an iterable object, which is a type of object that contains a sequence of values that can be stepped through value by value (iterated over).

Sentinels
A sentinel is a special value that marks the end of a sequence of items. When program reaches a sentinel, it knows that the end of the sequence of items was reached, and the loop terminates.
The sentinel must be distinctive enough so as not to be mistaken for a regular value in the sequence.
In Python, usually sequences are iterated through with for loops which automatically control for the size of the sequence. However, if we are taking in input we may not know how long the input actually is and we need some way of recognizing that the input process is finished. We can use a sentinel for this.
data = []

while value := int(input("Enter a non-negative number or enter -1 to finish: ")) != -1:
    if value < 0:
        print("Enter only non-negative numbers or -1 to finish.")
        continue
    else:
        data.append(value)
This code takes in non-negative numbers into a list called data. Note that the sentinel value is -1 and that any other negative value is ignored. This is an example of input validation. Input validation is a necessary part of programming as the computer cannot tell the difference between good data and bad data inherently.
If a user provides bad input, the program will likely produce bad output. This is the Garbage In, Garbage Out (GIGO) principle. So it is important to design programs in a way that bad input is not accepted. We do this through input validation, where we inspect the input before it is actually processed by the program.
This is common accomplished using a while loop like in the example above. The input process will repeat if the data is bad (usually with some error message displayed).

text:
Matrix Multiplication
When it comes to “multiplication” of matrices, we need to define what multiplication means. Without prior knowledge, most people would define matrix multiplication similarly to scalar multiplication. That is, element-wise multiplication.
This kind of multiplication is the Hadamard product which we have seen with vectors. And this is not generally what people mean when they say matrix multiplication.
In NumPy, the Hadamard product is computed using the asterisk.

The Hadamard Product

It is a very common beginner’s mistake to use the Hadamard product when you instead needed standard matrix multiplication.


A = np.array([
[1, 2, 3],
[4, 5, 6]
])

print(A * A)

[[ 1  4  9]
 [16 25 36]]




Matrix-Vector Multiplication
Let a matrix A be defined by
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 \\
2 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
Let a vector x be defined by
x =
\begin{bmatrix}
2  \\
5
\end{bmatrix}
Then we have
Ax = 2
\begin{bmatrix}
1  \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
+
5
\begin{bmatrix}
3  \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
What we have here is just an extension of scalar multiplication and vector addition. We can say that the matrix A is just storing column vectors and that the vector x tells us how much of each column to combine.

A = np.array([
[1,3],
[2,1]
])

x = np.array([2,5])

print(A @ x)

print(2*A[:,0] + 5*A[:,1])

[17  9]
[17  9]


Why not define multiplication some other way? Matrix multiplication was not invented to multiply tables of numbers. It was invented as a compact way to describe transformations of vectors. The chosen definition turns matrices into machines (or rules) that transform vectors.
Suppose an object has position (x,y) and you want to stretch the x-coordinate by 2 while leaving y unchanged.
What you want is a transformation that performs the following
\begin{bmatrix}
x  \\
y
\end{bmatrix}
\rightarrow
\begin{bmatrix}
2x  \\
y
\end{bmatrix}
We can go and write one operation that works for any values inside the vector. All we need to do is put the coefficients into a matrix.
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x  \\
y
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2x  \\
y
\end{bmatrix}
Using NumPy, we can verify this for chosen values of x and y .

vec = np.array([1,2]) #x = 1 and y = 2, so our scaled vector should be (2,2) if successful

mat = np.array([[2,0],
               [0,1]])

print(mat@vec)

[2 2]


Remember that a matrix a rule that we define whose purpose is to transform vectors.
We will reuse the matrix A defined earlier:
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 \\
2 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
And we will define vector x to be
x =
\begin{bmatrix}
a  \\
b
\end{bmatrix}
Let us rewrite A using the substitutions
c_1 =
\begin{bmatrix}
1  \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
,\;
c_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
3  \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
So we have
A =  
\begin{bmatrix}
c_1  & c_2
\end{bmatrix}
Then
Ax = ac_1 + bc_2
Note that the vector x tells us how much of each column to use. This is the meaning of matrix-vector multiplication, the matrix stores vectors and the input vector provides the weights.
Matrix columns can be viewed as directions or features, the entries of our vector is how much of each feature to use, and the output is the resulting combination.
This is very useful because many problems are linear combinations or can at least be approximated by linear combinations.


Matrix-Matrix Multiplication
If one matrix transforms vectors, what should happen when we apply two transformations in sequence?
Suppose that the matrix B rotates a vector x , then matrix A stretches it. We would like to have a single matrix that performs both operations at once, that is
A(Bx) = (AB)x
This requirement determines how matrix multiplication must work. Matrix multiplication is defined so that composing transformations works as expected.
If matrix C has columns C = \begin{bmatrix} c_1  & c_2 & c_3 \end{bmatrix} then multiplying C by matrix D gives us DC =\begin{bmatrix}Dc_1  & Dc_2 & Dc_3 \end{bmatrix}.
We can see that D is applied to every column of C. Matrix-matrix multiplication ultimately means we transform every column.
Computing the output of matrix multiplication is usually taught as the “row-column” approach.
For matrix
A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11}  & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{bmatrix}
and vector
x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}
we have
Ax = x_1 \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} \\ a_{21} \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} a_{12} \\ a_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1a_{11} + x_2a_{12} \\ x_1a_{21} + x_2a_{22} \end{bmatrix}
Note that we are using what amounts to the dot product here.
For matrix

B = \begin{bmatrix} 1  & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} 
and

C = \begin{bmatrix} 5  & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{bmatrix} 
BC =
\begin{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}
\\
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \times 5 + 2 \times 7 & 3 \times 5 + 4 \times 7 \\ 1 \times 6 + 2 \times 8 & 3 \times 6 + 4 \times 8 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 19 & 22 \\ 43 & 50 \end{bmatrix}

Confirm that for matrices B and C above that BC \neq CB.


Confirm by hand that the result of the matrix vector product in the Python example in the matrix-vector product subsection is in fact just the x value scaled by 2.



Dimension Rules
Matrix multiplication is not defined for any two arbitrary sized matrices.
An n \times p matrix takes a p-dimensional vector and produces an n-dimensional vector. Now, if we have an m \times n matix, this takes an n-dimensional vector and produces an m-dimensional vector.
If we have two transformations, the output dimension of the first transformation must equal the input dimension of the second transformation. We need to connect compatible transformations to have matrix multiplication defined. Looking at our matrices we have the m \times n matrix applied to the n \times p matrix. Writing this as (m \times n)(n \times p) we can see that the “inner” dimensions are equal here, and this is the requirement when it comes to matrix multiplication. The size of the output will be the “outer dimension” (m \times p).

title: 10: Matrices
text:
Rotation Matrices
A rotation matrix turns every vector by the same angle. To keep things simple, we will restrict ourselves to 2 dimensions.
The following matrix can rotate every point in our 2D space:
\begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta) & -sin(\theta) \\ \sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}
The simplicity of representing this transformation is one reason why graphics libraries use matrices everywhere.


Show Python plotting code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def rotate(theta,vector):

  rotation_matrix = np.array([

                    [np.cos(theta), -1*np.sin(theta)],

                    [np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta)]

                    ])

  return rotation_matrix @ vector

vector = [1,2]

theta = np.pi / 2

print(rotate(theta,vector))


[-2.  1.]


We can visualize the initial vector and its transformed version to confirm that our rotation matrix is working correctly.


Show Python plotting code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def setup_axes(ax, lim=3):
    """Create a consistent coordinate system."""
    ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim)
    ax.set_ylim(-lim, lim)

    ax.set_aspect('equal')

    # Draw coordinate axes
    ax.axhline(0, color='black', linewidth=1)
    ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=1)

    ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.4)

    ax.set_xlabel("x")
    ax.set_ylabel("y")

v = np.array([1,2])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,6))

setup_axes(ax)

# Vector
ax.quiver(0,0,v[0],v[1],
          angles='xy',
          scale_units='xy',
          scale=1)

# Components
ax.plot([0,v[0]],[0,0],'--')
ax.plot([v[0],v[0]],[0,v[1]],'--')

ax.text(v[0]+0.1,v[1]+0.1,"v = (1,2)")
plt.show()











Show Python plotting code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,6))

setup_axes(ax)

v = np.array([1,2])

angles = np.linspace(0,np.pi/2,2)

for theta in angles:

    R = np.array([
        [np.cos(theta),-np.sin(theta)],
        [np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta)]
    ])

    vr = R @ v

    if theta == 0:
        color = 'blue'
    else:
        color = 'red'
    ax.quiver(
        0,0,
        vr[0],vr[1],
        angles='xy',
        scale_units='xy',
        scale=1,
        alpha=0.7,
        color=color
    )    
plt.show()










Basis Vectors
We know we can decompose vectors into a representation based off of their constituent directions. For example, in 2D space we can use the x and y axes to fully describe any vector that lives in that space, that is, every vector in our space can be built from a linear combination of these directions. We then talk of the x and y components of the vector.
These building-block vectors are called basis vectors.


Show Python plotting code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,6))

setup_axes(ax)

e1 = np.array([1,0])
e2 = np.array([0,1])

ax.quiver(0,0,*e1,
          angles='xy',
          scale_units='xy',
          scale=1)

ax.quiver(0,0,*e2,
          angles='xy',
          scale_units='xy',
          scale=1)

ax.quiver(0,0,*v,
          angles='xy',
          scale_units='xy',
          scale=1)

ax.text(1.05,-0.15,"e₁")
ax.text(-0.2,1.1,"e₂")
ax.text(v[0]+0.1,v[1],"v")

plt.show()









The vector v in the plot can be viewed as 1e_1 + 2e_2.


Floating Point Approximations
Suppose we use our rotation matrix on the vector [1,0] where we rotate by \frac{\pi}{2}.
We would expect our output to be exactly [0,1] but sometimes we may see a slightly different answer.

vector = np.array([1,0])
theta = np.pi/2

R = np.array([
[np.cos(theta), -np.sin(theta)],
[np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta)]
])

print(R @ vector)

[6.123234e-17 1.000000e+00]


Because computers cannot store most real numbers exactly, they need to approximate them. This leads to small errors in the result. But, if we know that this is possible, we can work to control it.
For this example, we can clean up our answer using the round() method in NumPy.

np.round() takes in a NumPy array and an integer that controls the number of digits (the precision).


print(np.round(R @ vector, 10))

[0. 1.]


Here, we set the precision to 10 digits, which are all zeroes and so our rounded result is zero.

A series can be viewed as a single column in the DataFrame.

Index retrieval (idxmax(), idxmin()) tells you which label produced that maximum or minimum.

Note that there can be no text or NaN values in the columns that are cast into an array if you want to receive valid output.

pd.concat() is used when you have the exact same columns, but new rows of data. This works well for stacking multiple months, quarters, or batches of data together.
Note that it is important to reset the index to prevent repeated row numbers.
# Stacking Q1 and Q2 data vertically

full_year_df = pd.concat([q1_data, q2_data], axis=0)


#Reset the index so row numbers don't repeat

full_year_df = full_year_df.reset_index(drop=True)



Merges and joins are among the most important operations in pandas because they allow you to combine information from multiple DataFrames.
The important question when combining two DataFrames is: How do we know which rows belong together?
Pandas answers this by matching values in one or more columns. It can also match on an index, which is the term row label. Columns contain the actual data values; the index is just for identification.
pd.merge() combines two different DataFrames based on a shared column (a “Key”). This is identical to a SQL JOIN.

Left Join: Keep everything in the left table, attach data from the right table if it matches.
Right Join: Keep everything in the right table, attach data from the left table if it matches.
Inner Join: Keep only rows that appear in both tables.
Outer Join: Keep everything from both tables.

The basic syntax is:
pd.merge(left_df, #Left DataFrame

right_df, #Right DataFrame

on="ColumnName", #Column used for matching

how="inner") #Type of join
Suppose we have two DataFrames, customers and accounts.

customers = {
    'CustomerID':[101,102,103,104],
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie', 'David']
}

customers = pd.DataFrame(customers)

accounts = {
    'CustomerID':[101,101,103,105],
    'Name': ['2500', '1200', '8000', '500']
}

accounts = pd.DataFrame(accounts)



An inner join keeps only rows that appear in both tables.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="inner")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         103  Charlie   8000


Notice that Alice appears twice. This is because there are two matching rows in the Accounts table. Inner join is matching every possible pair.



A left join keeps everything from the left table.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="left")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         102      Bob    NaN
3         103  Charlie   8000
4         104    David    NaN


Since Bob and David have no entry in the right table (accounts) Pandas will insert NaN to fill the empty balance value.



A right join keeps everything from the right table.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="right")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         103  Charlie   8000
3         105      NaN    500


Note that customer 105 only exists in the accounts table; Pandas will insert NaN to fill the empty name value.



An outer join keeps everything from both tables.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="outer")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         102      Bob    NaN
3         103  Charlie   8000
4         104    David    NaN
5         105      NaN    500


Notice that nothing in either table is discarded.




Sometimes the key columns have different names.
This is easily handled using the left_on and right_on parameters.

pd.merge(customers, transactions, left_on="CustomerID", right_on="CustID")



Sometimes one column is not enough to guarantee a unique match.
For example, an Account Number might repeat across different Processing Dates. We can pass a list of columns to the on parameter to match on multiple keys simultaneously.
pd.merge(df1, df2, on=["CustomerID", "Type"])



A common mistake is confusing merge() with concat().
concat() stacks DataFrames together, it does not match rows. If you need to match rows, use merge() and specify the type of join.
If you want to match by the index (and not the data in the column) use the join() method instead. Matching by index is uncommon, most situations will be by matching columns.
If you do not need to match rows, use concat().

title: 14: Pandas
text:
Merges and joins are among the most important operations in pandas because they allow you to combine information from multiple DataFrames.
The important question when combining two DataFrames is: How do we know which rows belong together?
Pandas answers this by matching values in one or more columns. It can also match on an index, which is the term row label. Columns contain the actual data values; the index is just for identification.
pd.merge() combines two different DataFrames based on a shared column (a “Key”). This is identical to a SQL JOIN.

Left Join: Keep everything in the left table, attach data from the right table if it matches.
Right Join: Keep everything in the right table, attach data from the left table if it matches.
Inner Join: Keep only rows that appear in both tables.
Outer Join: Keep everything from both tables.

The basic syntax is:
pd.merge(left_df, #Left DataFrame

right_df, #Right DataFrame

on="ColumnName", #Column used for matching

how="inner") #Type of join
Suppose we have two DataFrames, customers and accounts.

customers = {
    'CustomerID':[101,102,103,104],
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie', 'David']
}

customers = pd.DataFrame(customers)

accounts = {
    'CustomerID':[101,101,103,105],
    'Name': ['2500', '1200', '8000', '500']
}

accounts = pd.DataFrame(accounts)



An inner join keeps only rows that appear in both tables.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="inner")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         103  Charlie   8000


Notice that Alice appears twice. This is because there are two matching rows in the Accounts table. Inner join is matching every possible pair.



A left join keeps everything from the left table.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="left")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         102      Bob    NaN
3         103  Charlie   8000
4         104    David    NaN


Since Bob and David have no entry in the right table (accounts) Pandas will insert NaN to fill the empty balance value.



A right join keeps everything from the right table.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="right")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         103  Charlie   8000
3         105      NaN    500


Note that customer 105 only exists in the accounts table; Pandas will insert NaN to fill the empty name value.



An outer join keeps everything from both tables.

merged = pd.merge(customers, accounts, on="CustomerID", how="outer")

print(merged)

   CustomerID   Name_x Name_y
0         101    Alice   2500
1         101    Alice   1200
2         102      Bob    NaN
3         103  Charlie   8000
4         104    David    NaN
5         105      NaN    500


Notice that nothing in either table is discarded.




Sometimes the key columns have different names.
This is easily handled using the left_on and right_on parameters.

pd.merge(customers, transactions, left_on="CustomerID", right_on="CustID")



Sometimes one column is not enough to guarantee a unique match.
For example, an Account Number might repeat across different Processing Dates. We can pass a list of columns to the on parameter to match on multiple keys simultaneously.
pd.merge(df1, df2, on=["CustomerID", "Type"])



A common mistake is confusing merge() with concat().
concat() stacks DataFrames together, it does not match rows. If you need to match rows, use merge() and specify the type of join.
If you want to match by the index (and not the data in the column) use the join() method instead. Matching by index is uncommon, most situations will be by matching columns.
If you do not need to match rows, use concat().

title: 12: Sets
text:
Sets
A set in Python is an object that stores a collection of data much in the same way as a set in mathematics is defined.

All items must be unique
Set is unordered
Elements can be of different data types

title: 12: Sets
text:
Creating a Set

For empty set, call set()
For non-empty set, call set(argument) where argument is an object that contains iterable elements.

e.g., argument can be a list, string, or tuple
If argument is a string, each character becomes a set element

For set of strings, pass them to the function as a list

If argument contains duplicates, only one of the duplicates will appear in the set



numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

print(numbers)

{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}



numbers = set([1,1,2,3,5])

print(numbers)

{1, 2, 3, 5}


Like many other objects in Python that we can iterate through, we can find the number of elements in a set using the len function.

numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

print(len(numbers))

5

title: 12: Sets
text:
Mutability
Sets are mutable objects just like lists, so we are able to add and remove elements associated with a set. However, since sets do not have order, there are not quite as many methods to do so since we are unable to use indices to specify a location in the set.

Adding Elements

add: adds an element to a set
update: adds multiple elements to a set

Argument must be a sequence containing iterable elements, and each of the elements is added to the set



numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

print(numbers)

{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}



numbers.add('six')

print(numbers)

{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 'six'}



numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

print(numbers)

{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}



numbers.update(['six','seven',8, 9])

print(numbers)

{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 'seven', 'six'}


The order you see from the print statement can change if you rerun the code. Remember that sets have no inherent order, this is just a visual representation of the contents.


Deleting Elements

removeand discard methods: delete the specified item from the set

The item that should be deleted is passed to both methods as an argument
These methods differently when the specified item is not found in the set

remove method raises a KeyError exception
discard method does not raise an exception


clear method: deletes all the elements of the set


numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

numbers.remove(1)

print(numbers)

{2, 3, 4, 5}



try:
     numbers.remove(6)
     print(numbers)

except Exception as e:
     print(e)

6



numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

numbers.discard(1)

print(numbers)

{2, 3, 4, 5}



numbers.discard(6)

print(numbers)

{2, 3, 4, 5}

text:
Using the for Loop, in, and not in Operators with Sets

A for loop can be used to iterate over elements in a set

General format: for item in set
The loop iterates once for each element in the set

The in operator can be used to test whether a value exists in a set

Similarly, the not in operator can be used to test whether a value does not exist in a set



numbers = set(list(range(1,6)))

for i in numbers:
     print(i)

title: 12: Sets
text:
Set Operations
For all the following set operations, the output of these methods returns a new set.

Union

The union of two sets is the set that contains all the elements of both sets.
To find the union of two sets:

Use the union method

Format: set1.union(set2)

Use the | operator

Format: set1 | set2




A = {1,2,3}

B = {2,3,4}

print(A | B)

{1, 2, 3, 4}




Intersection

The intersection of two sets is the set that contains only the elements found in both sets.
To find the intersection of two sets:

Use the intersection method

Format: set1.intersection(set2)

Use the & operator

Format: set1 & set2




A = {1,2,3}

B = {2,3,4}

print(A & B)

{2, 3}




Difference

The difference of two sets is the set that contains the elements that appear in the first set but do not appear in the second set.
To find the difference of two sets:

Use the difference method

Format: set1.difference(set2)

Use the - operator

Format: set1 - set2




A = {1,2,3}

B = {2,3,4}

print(A - B)

{1}




Symmetric Difference
The symmetric difference of two sets is the set that contains the elements that are not shared by the two sets.

To find the symmetric difference of two sets:

Use the symmetric_difference method

Format: set1.symmetric_difference(set2)

Use the ^ operator

Format: set1 ^ set2




A = {1,2,3}

B = {2,3,4}

print(A ^ B)

{1, 4}

text:
Subsets and Supersets

Set A is subset of set B if all the elements in set A are included in set B
To determine whether set A is subset of set B

Use the issubset method

Format: setA.issubset(setB)

Use the <= operator

Format: setA <= setB




A = {1,2,3}

B = {3,4}

print(B <= A)

False



A = {1,2,3}

B = {3}

print(B <= A)

True



Set A is superset of set B if it contains all the elements of set B
To determine whether set A is superset of set B

Use the issuperset method

Format: setA.issuperset(setB)

Use the >= operator

Format: setA>= setB




A = {1,2,3}

B = {3,4}

print(A >= B)

False



A = {1,2,3}

B = {3}

print(A >= B)

True

title: 12: Sets
text:
Set Comprehensions
Set comprehension: a concise expression that creates a new set by iterating over the elements of a sequence. Set comprehensions are written just like list comprehensions, except that a set comprehension is enclosed in curly braces {} instead of brackets []

Example: making a copy of a set


set1 = set([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

set2 = {item for item in set1}

print(id(set1),id(set2))

4625304256 4625306720



Example: creating a set that contains the squares of the numbers stored in another set


set1 = set([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

set2 = {item**2 for item in set1}

set2

{1, 4, 9, 16, 25}



Example: copying the numbers in a set that are less than 10


set1 = set([1, 20, 2, 40, 3, 50])

set2 = {item for item in set1 if item < 10}

set2

{1, 2, 3}

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
This course is about problem solving using computers. Problem solving means the ability to formulate problems, think creatively about solutions, and express a solution clearly and accurately. The process of learning to program is an excellent opportunity to practice problem solving skills.
Having a computer solve a problem requires the creation of a set of instructions, a program. A program is a sequence of instructions that specifies how to perform a computation. An individual instruction is referred to as a statement. And so a program is a collection of statements.
The computation might be something as complex as rendering an html page in a web browser or encoding a video and streaming it across the network. It can also be a symbolic computation, such as searching for and replacing text in a document or (strangely enough) compiling a program.
The process of creating these instructions is programming .


If problem solving is a central part of computer science, then the solutions that you create through the problem solving process are also important. In computer science, we refer to these solutions as algorithms. 
An algorithm is a step-by-step list of instructions that if followed exactly will solve the problem under consideration. Our goal is to take a problem and develop an algorithm that can serve as a general solution. Once we have such a solution, we can use our computer to automate the execution.
Programming is a skill that allows us to take an algorithm and represent it in a notation (a program) that can be followed by a computer. These programs are written in programming languages .

text:
Storing Characters
All characters are converted to a numeric code and this numeric code is stored in memory.
The most fundamental coding scheme is ASCII but it is limited to only 128 different characters.
A more modern replacement is called Unicode which is both compatible with ASCII and can represent many more characters.

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Other Types of Data
The word digital describes anything that stores data as binary numbers
For example digital images are composed of pixels. And to store these images, each pixel is converted to a binary number representing the pixel’s color.
Similarly, digital music is composed of sections called samples. To store this music, each sample is converted to a binary number.

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Type of Errors
Three kinds of errors can occur in a program: 

Syntax Errors
Runtime Errors
Semantic Errors
crumbs: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Syntax Errors
Python can only execute a program if the program is syntactically correct ; otherwise, the process fails and returns an error message.  Syntax refers to the structure of a program and the rules about that structure.
For example, in English, a sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with a period. If there is a single syntax error anywhere in your program, Python will display an error message and quit. You will not be able to complete the execution of your program.
During the first few weeks of your programming career, you will probably spend a lot of time tracking down syntax errors. However, as you gain experience, you will make fewer errors, and you will also be able to find your errors faster.
crumbs: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Runtime Errors
The second type of error is a runtime error, so called because the error does not appear until you run the program. These errors are also called exceptions because they usually indicate that something exceptional (and bad) has happened. Runtime errors are rare in the simple programs you will see in the first few chapters, so it might be a while before you encounter one.
crumbs: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Semantic Errors
If there is a semantic error in your program, it will run successfully in the sense that the computer will not generate any error messages. However, your program will not do the right thing. It will do something else. Specifically, it will do exactly what you told it to do.
The problem is that the program you wrote is not the program you wanted to write. The meaning of the program (its semantics) is wrong.
Identifying semantic errors can be tricky because it requires you to work backward by looking at the output of the program and trying to figure out what it is doing.
crumbs: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Parsing and Semantics
When you read a sentence in English or a statement in a formal language, you have to figure out what the structure of the sentence is. This process is called parsing. For example, when you hear the sentence, “The other shoe fell”, you understand that the other shoe is the subject and fell is the verb. Once you have parsed a sentence, you can figure out what it means, or the semantics of the sentence.

section: Differences between Formal and Natural Languages
text:
Differences between Formal and Natural Languages
Although formal and natural languages have many features in common like tokens, structure, syntax, and semantics, there are substantial differences.

Ambiguity

Natural languages are full of ambiguity, which people deal with by using contextual clues and other information.
Formal languages are designed to be nearly or completely unambiguous, which means that any statement has exactly one meaning, regardless of context.

Redundancy

In order to make up for ambiguity and reduce misunderstandings, natural languages employ lots of redundancy.
As a result, natural languages are often verbose. Formal languages are less redundant and more concise.

Literalness

Formal languages mean exactly what they say.
Natural languages are full of idiom and metaphor.
If someone says, “The other shoe fell”, there is probably no shoe and nothing falling.

text:
Interactive Mode
When you start Python in interactive mode, you will see a prompt. This indicates the interpreter is waiting for a Python statement to be typed.
The prompt reappears after previous statement is executed and (in general) an error message displayed if you incorrectly type a statement.
Interactive mode is a good way to quickly practice simple new parts of Python but becomes cumbersome quickly for more complicated tasks.

Writing Python Programs and Running Them in Script Mode
For our course we will use script mode which allows us to save programs for future purposes.
To create a program, use script mode:

Save a set of Python statements in a file
The filename should have the .py extension
To run the file, or script, type python filenameat the operating system command line or open the file through your IDE

text:
Basic Programming Instructions

Input

Get data from the keyboard, a file, or some other device.

Output

Display data on the screen or send data to a file or other device.

Math and Logic

Perform basic mathematical operations like addition and multiplication and logical operations like and, or, and not.

Conditional execution

Check for certain conditions and execute the appropriate sequence of statements.

Repetition

Perform some action repeatedly, usually with some variation.


These basic instructions comprise nearly everything used in programming.
Every program you have ever used, no matter how complicated, is made up of instructions that look like these. 
We can describe programming as the process of breaking a large, complex task into smaller and smaller subtasks until the subtasks are simple enough to be performed with sequences of these basic instructions.

Hello World
Traditionally, the first program written in a new language is called Hello, World because all it does is display the words, Hello, World.

This is an example of using the print function, which displays a value on the screen.

print('Hello world')

Hello world



The print function will be one of the most common functions we use in this course as it is extremely useful for seeing what it happening step-by-step as your program executes.

text:
Comments
As programs get bigger and more complicated, they get more difficult to read. Formal languages are dense, and it is often difficult to look at a piece of code and figure out what it is doing, or why.
For this reason, it is a good idea to add notes to your programs to explain in natural language what the program is doing. These notes are called comments.
A comment in a computer program is text that is intended only for the human reader, it is completely ignored by the interpreter.

In Python, the # token starts a comment. The rest of the line is ignored. Here is a new version of Hello, World!.

print('Hello world') #This is a comment

Hello world
